topic.title: Ecological terms, fieldwork and quadrat sampling
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Two papers use this. B1 opens with an ecological-terms question built round a named habitat, and Unit 7 Booklet B Biology has set the six-mark QWC on estimating abundance in two of the last three Summer series. The terms carry [1] each, percentage cover [1]-[2], a mean [2], scaling up [3], and the QWC [6]. Almost every mark is a word rather than a difficulty.
mustMemorise: Habitat = the place where an organism lives
Population = all the organisms of ONE species in a habitat
Community = all the populations of all the species in a habitat
Ecosystem = the community plus the non-living surroundings
Biodiversity = the number of different species present
Abiotic factors: wind speed, water, pH, light, temperature
Random sampling = random numbers used as co-ordinates
Belt transect = quadrats at fixed intervals along a line across a habitat
Name the QUADRAT and use a KEY in every six-mark fieldwork answer
Estimate = mean per quadrat × (habitat area ÷ quadrat area)
notOnThisSpec: Capture-recapture and the Lincoln index for animal populations
Simpson's or any other diversity index
Pooters, pitfall traps, sweep nets, Tullgren funnels and kick sampling
Succession and zonation as named processes

externalRefs.credit: Freesciencelessons, GCSE Biology Revision "Required Practical 9: Sampling Organisms"

note.subject: science

Abiotic: wind speed, water, pH, light, temperature

mean = sum of counts ÷ number of quadrats

notOnThisSpec: Pooters, pitfall traps and sweep nets

mustBeAbleTo: Give the six ecological terms and tell them apart in a described habitat
Sort factors into biotic and abiotic and name the instrument for each abiotic one
Describe how to place a quadrat at random using random co-ordinates
Say why a belt transect is used, and that it is not random sampling
Read percentage cover from a gridded quadrat
Calculate a mean from repeated quadrat counts
Scale a mean up to a whole habitat using the quadrat area
Name the quadrat and the identification key in a six-mark method
Explain that repeats improve reliability, not accuracy
Suggest ways of increasing biodiversity, rather than defining it
sheet.howExamined: B1 Foundation (60 marks, 1 hour) for the terms and factors, and Unit 7 Practical Skills Booklet B Biology (35 marks, 30 minutes) for the practical, where this has been the 6-mark QWC in two of the last three Summer series. Calculator allowed in both. Terms carry [1] each and are asked as separate parts. Booklet B builds a whole question round one habitat: name an abiotic factor, name the instrument, the QWC method, a tally table, a bar chart and a trend.
traps: Confusing population, community and ecosystem (March 2026 B1 F Q6 and B1 H Q1)
Giving a living factor when an abiotic one is asked for
Offering a thermostat instead of a thermometer (Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B)
Never naming the apparatus as a quadrat (Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B)
Leaving out the identification key in the six-mark method (Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B)
Choosing quadrat positions yourself, or calling a transect random sampling
Scaling the total rather than the mean, or forgetting to divide by the quadrat area
Defining biodiversity when asked how to increase it (March 2026 B1 F Q6)
Saying repeats improve accuracy rather than reliability

Filling in a tally chart without following the pattern already printed in it: a few candidates lost that mark even though worked rows were there in the same table to copy (Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B Q3)

steps.decision: Always start with the mean per quadrat. Put the whole sum in brackets on the calculator, or the division happens before the addition.

steps.working: Number of quadrat areas in the field = (40 × 25) ÷ 0.25 = 1000 ÷ 0.25 = 4000
steps.decision: The quadrat is 0.5 m square, so its area is 0.25 m², not 1 m². Dividing the field area by the quadrat area is the step people skip.
Multiply the mean by the number of quadrat areas. Check the size of the answer: tens of thousands is right for a small plant in a field this size.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The mean is 6 daisies per quadrat. The field is 1000 m² and each quadrat covers 0.25 m², so 4000 quadrats would fit. The estimate is 6 × 4000 = 24000 daisies.

steps.working: Lay two tape measures along two edges of the field at right angles and use pairs of random numbers as co-ordinates.
steps.decision: Say how the randomness is produced. 'Randomly' on its own is a claim; random numbers used as co-ordinates is a method.

steps.working: Place a quadrat of known area at the first pair of co-ordinates.
steps.decision: Name the apparatus. Summer 2025 examiners reported candidates who had done the practical but could not name the quadrat.

steps.working: Use an identification key to work out which plants inside the quadrat are daisies.
steps.decision: This is the point almost nobody wrote. A key is how you know which species you are counting.

steps.working: Count the daisies inside the quadrat and record the number in a results table.
steps.decision: Counting and recording are separate indicative points in the scheme.

steps.working: Repeat at several more random positions.
steps.decision: Repeats are what make the estimate reliable rather than a single lucky square.

steps.working: Calculate the mean number per quadrat, then multiply by the number of quadrat areas that fit in the field.
steps.decision: Finish with the arithmetic that turns your samples into an estimate for the whole field.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Lay two tape measures along two edges of the field at right angles and generate pairs of random numbers to use as co-ordinates. Place a quadrat of known area at the first pair of co-ordinates. Use an identification key to decide which plants inside the frame are daisies, count them, and record the number in a results table. Repeat at several more random positions, calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat, and multiply that mean by the number of quadrat areas that fit into the field to estimate the total.

twin.stem: Describe how you would find out whether buttercups are more common at the edge of a wood than in the middle of it.

accepted: lay a belt transect from the edge of the wood into the middle, place a quadrat at fixed intervals along the line, use a key to identify the buttercups, count them in each quadrat, record the results and compare the mean number at the edge with the mean number in the middle

items.stem: All the different species of plants and animals living in a rock pool, taken together, are called
items.skill: Tell the six ecological terms apart

options.feedback: A community: every population in that habitat. Add the water, rock and light and you have the ecosystem.
A population is one species only. All the species together is the community.
The habitat is the rock pool itself — the place. The organisms in it form the community.
Very close. An ecosystem is the community plus the non-living surroundings it interacts with.

items.stem: Which of these is an abiotic factor?

options.feedback: Light is one of the five abiotic factors the specification names, along with wind speed, water, pH and temperature.
That is biodiversity, which is a biotic factor — it is about living things.
Rabbits are alive, so this is biotic. Abiotic factors are the non-living conditions.

options.text: the amount of grazing by sheep
options.feedback: Grazing is done by living animals, so it is biotic.

items.stem: Which method gives a fair estimate of how many daisies are in a whole field?

options.text: quadrats placed at co-ordinates taken from random numbers
options.feedback: Random numbers as co-ordinates give every part of the field the same chance of being sampled.

options.text: quadrats placed wherever there are plenty of daisies
options.feedback: That guarantees an overestimate. The whole point of random sampling is to take the choice away from you.

options.text: quadrats placed every five metres along one line
options.feedback: That is a belt transect. It shows how a species changes across a habitat, but it does not sample the whole field fairly.

options.text: one quadrat placed in the middle of the field
options.feedback: One quadrat gives no mean and no way of spotting an unusual patch. Several positions are needed.

items.stem: In a six-mark answer on estimating plant abundance, which step do most candidates leave out?

options.text: using an identification key to name the species
options.feedback: Exactly this. Summer 2025 examiners reported that few candidates mentioned a key, even though they had done the practical.

options.text: counting the plants inside the quadrat
options.feedback: Almost everybody writes the counting. The step that disappears is identifying the species with a key.
Recording is usually there. Identifying with a key is the one that is missing.
Repeats are usually there too. Try again: what tells you which plant is which?

items.stem: A quadrat of side 0.5 m gives a mean of 6 daisies. How do you scale that up to a field of 1000 m²?
items.skill: Scale up using the quadrat area

options.feedback: The field holds 4000 quadrat areas, so the estimate is 24000.
That would be right only if the quadrat covered 1 m². It covers 0.25 m², so this answer is four times too small.
That gives an area per daisy, not a number of daisies. Multiply the mean by how many quadrats would fit.
Multiplying by a number smaller than one makes the estimate smaller than a single quadrat's count, which cannot be right.

items.stem: A student repeats the quadrat count at ten positions instead of one. What does this improve?

options.feedback: Repeats let you take a mean and spot an odd result, which is reliability. Accuracy is a different idea.
Each count is just as accurate as before. Repeating makes the overall estimate more reliable.
Validity is about whether the method answers the question asked. Repeating improves reliability.
Resolution is the smallest change an instrument can show. Counting whole plants does not change with repeats.

context.setting: A hedgerow beside a barley field, with its own plants and animals

parts.stem:
A hedgerow contains hawthorn, bramble, wrens, field mice and many insects.
Name the ecological term for all the wrens living in the hedgerow.

scheme.for: population

hints: One species, one place.
parts.workedSolution: A population.

commonErrors.feedback: A community is every species together and an ecosystem adds the non-living surroundings. One species in one place is a population.

parts.stem: Name the ecological term for all the plants and animals living in the hedgerow, taken together.

scheme.for: community

hints: Every population added together.
parts.workedSolution: A community.

commonErrors.feedback: An ecosystem includes the soil, water and light as well. A habitat is the place itself. All the living things together form the community.

parts.stem: Define the term biodiversity.

accepted: the number of different species of plants and animals present

scheme.for: the number of different species (of plants and animals) present
scheme.examinerNote: Counting organisms is not counting species.

hints: It counts kinds, not individuals.
parts.workedSolution: Biodiversity is the number of different species of plants and animals present.

commonErrors.feedback: Biodiversity counts how many different species there are, not how many individuals.

context.setting: A group measuring conditions on a sand dune before counting the plants

parts.stem:
A group measures the temperature of the sand at each sampling point.
State whether temperature is a biotic or an abiotic factor.

scheme.for: abiotic

hints: Is temperature alive?
parts.workedSolution: Abiotic.

parts.stem: Name one other abiotic factor they could measure on the dune.

scheme.for: wind speed / light (intensity) / water or moisture content / pH
scheme.examinerNote: The specification names wind speed, water, pH, light and temperature.

hints: Five are named in the specification, and you have used one of them.
parts.workedSolution: Wind speed (or light intensity, water content, or pH).

commonErrors.feedback: That is a living factor, so it is biotic. Abiotic factors are the non-living conditions: wind speed, water, pH, light and temperature.

parts.stem: Name the instrument used to measure the factor you gave in part (b).

scheme.for: anemometer (wind speed) / light meter (light) / pH meter or pH probe (pH) / balance (water content by drying and reweighing)
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B: a few candidates gave a thermostat, which controls a temperature rather than measuring one.

hints: Each abiotic factor has its own named instrument.
parts.workedSolution: An anemometer measures wind speed. (A light meter measures light, a pH meter measures pH, and a balance is used to find water content by drying and reweighing.)

commonErrors.feedback: A thermostat controls a temperature; it does not measure a factor. Name the measuring instrument.

parts.stem:
The quadrat is divided into 100 small squares. The shaded squares show where clover covers the ground.
Use the diagram to find the percentage cover of clover.

scheme.for: counts 37 shaded squares

scheme.examinerNote: With 100 squares the count and the percentage are the same number; state the percentage, not just the count.

hints: There are 100 squares, so each one is worth 1%.
parts.workedSolution: 37 squares out of 100 are shaded, so the percentage cover is 37 ÷ 100 × 100 = 37%.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the number of squares the clover does NOT cover. Count the shaded squares.

parts.stem: State one advantage of measuring percentage cover rather than counting individual plants.

accepted: clover grows as a mat so the individual plants cannot be told apart, but the cover can still be measured

scheme.for: some plants (grasses, mosses, clover) grow in mats so individuals cannot be distinguished / counting would be too slow

hints: Try counting individual grass plants in a lawn.
parts.workedSolution: Clover, grasses and mosses grow as spreading mats, so individual plants cannot be told apart and cannot be counted; percentage cover can still be measured.

parts.stem:
The 10 quadrat counts were 7, 4, 9, 6, 3, 8, 5, 6, 4, 8.
Calculate the mean number of daisies per quadrat.
Show your working out.

scheme.for: adds the counts to give 60
divides by 10 to give 6
scheme.examinerNote: ecf from an arithmetic slip in the addition.

hints: Brackets round the whole sum before you divide.

commonErrors.feedback: 60 is the total of the ten counts. The mean is that total divided by 10.

parts.stem:
The field measures 40 m by 25 m and each quadrat has sides of 0.5 m.
Calculate an estimate of the total number of daisies in the field.
Show your working out.

scheme.for: field area 40 × 25 = 1000 m² and quadrat area 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 m²
number of quadrat areas = 1000 ÷ 0.25 = 4000

scheme.examinerNote: ecf from the mean in part (a).

hints: The quadrat covers 0.25 m², not 1 m².
How many quadrats would fit into the field?
parts.workedSolution: Field area = 40 × 25 = 1000 m². Quadrat area = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 m². Number of quadrat areas = 1000 ÷ 0.25 = 4000. Estimated total = 6 × 4000 = 24000 daisies.

commonErrors.feedback: The mean has been multiplied by the field area in square metres. Each quadrat covers 0.25 m², so 4000 of them fit, not 1000.
The total of the ten counts has been scaled up instead of the mean, so the answer is ten times too big.

parts.stem: Suggest one reason why the answer to part (b) is only an estimate.

accepted: only a small part of the field was actually sampled, so the daisies may not be spread evenly across the rest of it

scheme.for: only a sample of the field was counted and the daisies may not be evenly distributed
accept: the quadrats may have landed on unusual patches

hints: What fraction of the field was actually looked at?
parts.workedSolution: Only 10 quadrats were counted out of the 4000 that would fit, and daisies are not spread evenly, so scaling up from that sample gives an estimate rather than a true count.

accepted: the number of plantain plants decreases as the distance from the footpath increases, from 9 down to 1

scheme.for: the number decreases as the distance from the path increases

hints: Use the words 'as' and 'increases' or 'decreases'.
parts.workedSolution: The number of plantain plants decreases as the distance from the footpath increases, falling from 9 at the path to 1 at the hedge.

parts.stem: Explain this trend, using the light readings.

accepted: the light falls from 950 lux at the path to 200 lux at the hedge, and with less light there is less photosynthesis so fewer plantain plants can grow

scheme.for: the light intensity falls from 950 lux to 200 lux because the hedge shades the ground
with less light there is less photosynthesis, so fewer plantain plants survive there

Then say what light is for.

parts.stem: Explain why a belt transect was used here instead of random sampling.

accepted: the question is about how the plants change with distance from the path, and a transect places quadrats in a line across that change, while random sampling would only give one overall estimate

any: from the path to the hedge

scheme.for: the investigation is about how the plants change across the habitat, so quadrats are needed in a line at measured distances
random sampling would estimate the total number but would not show the pattern with distance

hints: Ask what each method is designed to find out.
parts.workedSolution: The investigation asks how the plantain changes with distance from the path, so the quadrats have to be at known distances in a line — that is what a belt transect gives. Use the key. A plant in the quadrat has leaves made of three leaflets.
Identify the plant.

scheme.for: clover

hints: Start at question 1 of the key.
parts.workedSolution: Clover.

parts.stem:
A second plant has broad leaves and flowers with white petals around a yellow centre.
Identify this plant.

scheme.for: daisy

hints: Work down the key: not three leaflets, not long and narrow, petals not yellow and shiny.
parts.workedSolution: Daisy.

parts.stem: Explain why the group needed a key before they could count the daisies in each quadrat.

accepted: the key lets them tell which plants are daisies and which are other species, so they only count the right species and their results are valid

so only the species being investigated is counted and the results are valid
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 U7 Booklet B: few candidates mentioned a key at all.

hints: What would happen if a buttercup were counted as a daisy?
parts.workedSolution: A quadrat usually holds several similar-looking species. The key lets the group work out which plants are daisies and which are not, so only daisies are counted and the estimate is a valid measure of the daisy population rather than a mixture of species.

context.setting: Two groups comparing methods after the same fieldwork trip

parts.stem:
One group used three quadrats and another used twelve.
Explain which group's estimate is more reliable, and why.

accepted: the group with twelve quadrats, because a mean from more samples is less affected by one unusual patch of ground

scheme.for: the group that used twelve quadrats
a mean taken from more samples is less affected by one unusually empty or crowded patch

hints: Which mean would change most if one quadrat landed on a bare patch?
parts.workedSolution: The group with twelve quadrats. A mean calculated from twelve samples is less affected by one unusually crowded or empty patch of ground than a mean from three, so the estimate is more reliable.

commonErrors.feedback: More samples improve reliability. Accuracy is how close a single measurement is to the true value, and that depends on how carefully you count, not on how often.

parts.stem:
One student counted every plant in the quadrat, including those whose stems were outside the frame but whose leaves reached inside.
Suggest why this makes the results less valid.

accepted: the rule for what counts was not the same every time, so the counts are not comparable and the estimate no longer measures the number of plants rooted in that area

scheme.for: the rule for deciding what is inside the quadrat was not applied consistently
so the counts are not comparable with the other quadrats and the total will be an overestimate

hints: A fair count needs the same rule in every quadrat.
parts.workedSolution: The decision about what counts as being inside the frame has to be the same in every quadrat. Counting plants rooted outside it in some quadrats and not others makes the counts inconsistent, so they cannot be compared and the scaled-up total is too high.

parts.stem: State what should be done with an anomalous quadrat count before the mean is calculated.

accepted: it should be left out of the mean, and repeated if possible

scheme.for: leave it out of the mean (and repeat that reading if possible)

hints: An anomaly is a reading that does not fit the pattern.
parts.workedSolution: An anomalous count is left out when the mean is calculated, and the reading is repeated if there is time.

commonErrors.feedback: An anomalous reading is excluded from the mean. Including it drags the mean away from the true value.

context.setting: A woodland being managed to bring more species back

parts.stem:
Beside a footpath there were 9 plantain plants per quadrat. Under the hedge there was 1.
Calculate the percentage decrease from the path to the hedge.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: decrease = 9 − 1 = 8
divides by the ORIGINAL value: 8 ÷ 9 × 100

scheme.examinerNote: March 2026 B1 H: some divided by the incorrect denominator and gained only partial credit.

hints: Percentage decrease = decrease ÷ starting value × 100.
The starting value is the count at the path.
parts.workedSolution: Decrease = 9 − 1 = 8. Percentage decrease = 8 ÷ 9 × 100 = 88.9%.

commonErrors.feedback: Divided by the final value instead of the starting value. A percentage decrease can never be more than 100%, so 800% is a signal that the denominator is wrong.

parts.stem: Suggest two things that could be done to increase the biodiversity of a woodland.

accepted: plant a mixture of native tree and shrub species, and leave dead wood and leaf litter on the ground as habitats for insects and fungi

scheme.for: any two from: plant a mixture of native tree and shrub species / leave dead wood and leaf litter as habitats / dig a pond / cut back a dense canopy to let light reach the woodland floor / remove an invasive species / put up nest boxes — [1] each

context.setting: A class asked to find out how many buttercups grow on a rugby pitch

parts.stem:
A class is asked to estimate the number of buttercup plants growing on a rugby pitch.
Describe how they should carry out this investigation.

Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: place a square frame called a quadrat on the ground
choose each position at random, using pairs of random numbers as co-ordinates along two tape measures
use an identification key to work out which plants are buttercups
count the buttercup plants inside the quadrat
record each count in a results table
repeat at several more random positions
calculate the mean number of buttercups per quadrat
scale the mean up using the area of the pitch and the area of the quadrat

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Name the apparatus in your first sentence: quadrat.
Two points almost everyone forgets: the key, and the mean.
parts.workedSolution: Lay two tape measures along two edges of the pitch at right angles and generate pairs of random numbers to use as co-ordinates. Place a quadrat, a square frame of known area, at the first pair of co-ordinates. Use an identification key to decide which of the plants inside the frame are buttercups, count them, and record the number in a results table. Repeat the whole process at several more random positions. Calculate the mean number of buttercups per quadrat, then multiply that mean by the number of quadrat areas that fit into the pitch to estimate the total number of buttercups.

commonErrors.feedback: The key is missing. Examiners reported it as the point almost nobody wrote: you cannot count a species until you know which plants belong to it.
Choosing the spots yourself always overestimates. Use random numbers as co-ordinates so every part of the pitch has the same chance.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciara is asked: 'Describe how you would estimate the number of daisies in a field. [6]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: I would walk around the field and find a good patch of daisies.
I would put the square frame down there and count the daisies inside it.
I would do that three more times and add up all the numbers.
Then I would multiply the total by the area of the field in square metres.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Choosing a **good patch** is the opposite of random sampling: it guarantees an overestimate, and the mark for random placement is lost at the first line. Three more problems follow. The frame is never named as a **quadrat**, no **key** is used to identify the plants, and the last line scales the **total** rather than the **mean**, and multiplies by the field area rather than by the number of **quadrat areas** that fit into it.
correction: I would lay two tape measures along two edges of the field and use pairs of random numbers as co-ordinates.
I would place a quadrat at the first pair of co-ordinates, use a key to identify the daisies, count them and record the number.
I would repeat at several more random positions and calculate the mean number per quadrat.
Then I would multiply the mean by the field area divided by the area of the quadrat.
findTheMistake.feedback: About two of six as written: counting and repeating are there, but the method is not a sampling method. Two habits rescue this answer. First, never let yourself choose the spot — write 'random numbers used as co-ordinates' every time. Second, name the apparatus and the key in your first two sentences, because examiners report both as the points that go missing.

prompts.answer: A population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat. A community is all the populations of all the species in that habitat. An ecosystem is the community together with the non-living surroundings it interacts with.
The number of different species of plants and animals present.

prompts.prompt: Name the five abiotic factors the specification lists, and one instrument for each.
prompts.answer: Wind speed (anemometer), water content (balance, by drying and reweighing), pH (pH meter), light (light meter) and temperature (thermometer).

prompts.prompt: How do you place a quadrat at random?
prompts.answer: Lay two tape measures along two edges at right angles, generate pairs of random numbers and use each pair as a co-ordinate for one quadrat position.

prompts.prompt: When do you use a belt transect rather than random sampling?
prompts.answer: When you want to know how a species changes across a habitat — from a path to a hedge, or up a beach. A transect is not random sampling.

prompts.prompt: Which two things do examiners say go missing from the six-mark fieldwork answer?
prompts.answer: The name of the apparatus — the quadrat — and the use of a key to identify the species. Write both in your first two sentences.

prompts.prompt: How do you scale a mean quadrat count up to a whole field?
prompts.answer: Multiply the mean number per quadrat by the area of the field divided by the area of the quadrat.

prompts.prompt: Does repeating a quadrat count improve reliability or accuracy?
prompts.answer: Reliability. Repeats allow a mean and show up an anomalous result. Accuracy is how close a single measurement is to the true value, and depends on how carefully you count.
